turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How did ACT UP respond to this information? What did they decide to do?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: They essentially accepted it and put it on their agenda. That was it. It was on the agenda.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What were the drugs that people wanted to have studied?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I can’t remember all the drugs, but there were at least five or six drugs. They all have the letters and stuff. I can remember the AL very clearly, because I helped distribute it. But, the others –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did any of them turn out to be valuable?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, I don’t think so. But, some of them were cancer drugs, too. They were not in the nucleoside area. They were not that type of a drug, but they were cancer drugs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Where did you fit in, in ACT UP? Did you get into a committee? Or, did you start a committee?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, I started a committee. It was going to these meetings. It wasn’t just going to ACT UP. There were meetings after ACT UP, after the general meeting.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, Monday night, after the general meeting?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Right, right. There were meetings at people’s houses. I can’t remember his name – Herbert – you probably know who I mean – I don’t know – you’re probably interviewing him. Herb – anyway, he made his house available, and people went to his house, and we all discussed what we should do next, with respect to treatment. And, actually – I can’t remember the names – a little guy and I – we decided we needed a treatment committee, and he said, no, we need treatment and we need data. So, it became the Treatment Data Committee. So, we formed the committee and that was –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Who were some of the people on the Treatment and Data Committee?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Jim Eigo, of course, was in it. But, he came a little later. He was at Herb’s house. He was there. And, there were a number of other people. I can’t remember their names at this point. David Kirschenbaum was the other. And so, we formed a committee, and it met every week, and we worked on it. I worked on it all day long, actually. We were calling drug companies and things like that – finding out, here’s a drug, let’s find out where it is, how can we get it? And, so forth. So, we had a list of drugs that we were working on – the DHPG. Then, we had an action in Washington and so forth.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What was the action?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: The action for DHPG was at a hearing.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Let’s go through the whole trajectory, so people can understand how the whole process worked in ACT UP. So, first you identified DHPG, and, were there any trials for it?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I would say there were trials for it, but they probably were very small.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Let’s say what the drug was for, also.

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It’s for CMV retinitis. So the idea is, number one, it should be an approved drug. Before we even had this Treatment and Data Committee, we had had sessions where we started to learn what the FDA was all about. And, I can remember a group of us trying to teach one another what the FDA is about, and how the FDA works to approve drugs. That was a very key part of the whole thing. It wasn’t only the testing of drugs, the clinical trials – but how these drugs would be approved, and would they be approved in a timely way? Because they were not being approved in a timely way. And, DHPG was one of the drugs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, you felt confident that this was a drug that definitely merited approval.

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Oh yeah, everyone said that it definitely merited approval.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And what held it up? What was the problem?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It was the whole process of the FDA.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: That they had no –

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It was the bureaucracy of the review. On the application they have tons of paper they have to go through, and so forth. They have committees that will review the data and so forth. An anti-viral committee would review it. It would have to be put on a calendar. They would have to look at the data, make presentations. But, the whole process was very slow. And, the drug companies agreed, everything was slow. They agreed too, so they had an ally in us.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Who was the company?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I can’t remember. I guess it was –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Glaxo?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Burroughs Wellcome? I’m not certain.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So what would be the process? So, first you would go to the FDA?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Because there was another new, purine type compound.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, first did you go to the FDA and say look, this is ridiculous, how can you speed this up?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, there was contact with the –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Who were the people there that you were in contact with?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Ellen Cooper, and different people.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What was their response?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: They met and we had to put pressure on them. There was constant pressure on them. It was not only us in ACT UP New York. There were other people putting pressure on them, too.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, this action was part of that pressure?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, that was at a meeting – at an advisory committee meeting – and I can remember we had clocks – made clocks. Paper clocks or cardboard clocks, to show that the time was going by and so forth.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, after you disrupted a meeting at FDA about DHPG – had you ever done anything like that before in your life?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, but everybody was gung-ho on doing it.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did you feel scared?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. A little. Not much.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Were they angry?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. They were somewhat I would say stunned.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, how long after that did DHPG get released?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I really don’t know the exact time, but it was made available and some key people got the drug. They were key – Michael Callen – a number that I knew.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, Michael Callen’s sight was saved –

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It wasn’t Michael Callen, exactly, but a friend of his, who had CMV retinitis.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, were you involved in ACT UP’s restructuring of the FDA approval system? The parallel track system? Can you tell us a little bit about who thought of that, and how it was implemented? What it was?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I’ve talked about it so much. I can’t figure out right now. I talked about it – I can remember talking about parallel track, but right now, I can’t think –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: You can’t remember what it was?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It’s getting the one drug – I can’t remember how it went, at this point.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Was that Jim Eigo’s project?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah. He talked about it quite a bit. We all talked about it.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Why did ACT UP have to think of a way for the FDA to be more effective? How come the FDA couldn’t deal with it?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: They had their bureaucracy – the way they did things, how they got doctors. I mean, you know – within their ranks, there – they came from major medical centers. They weren’t looking to make the system work better. That wasn’t their job, number one. They would say, that’s somebody else’s job. This is what developed for them. They didn’t think of making the system more effective, I don’t think.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How do you think that people in ACT UP got to the point, where they realized that they had to and could be the people who were going to restructure the FDA?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I don’t think they thought that they were doing this, but they knew that they had to put pressure on the FDA and change the FDA – how they did business, because the drug development system was just taking too long. There was too much bureaucracy. Trials couldn’t be done, because of the FDA. Drugs couldn’t be approved and gotten by the public or whatever because of this long process. The compassionate use was not an effective way to get drugs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Was compassionate use another ACT UP –

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Because the compassionate use – yeah. The whole idea of getting the drugs before they were approved and expanding them to communities, before the exact approval date, that they knew the drugs were working and the expanded access thing.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And do you remember who thought of that?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It’s hard to say one person, because we were all working on this together, and we just said, well, this is what we have to do. We have to get these drugs sooner. They have to be available to people – people who have no other choices. They have to be available. So, it just sort of mushroomed and developed. I can’t remember the exact person who had this idea or that idea, because we were working on various aspects of it. We knew FDA was key. We knew that NIAID was key. And, there were people who were putting a lot of energy in each one of these segments of the puzzle.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Now, when ACT UP did its famous action at the FDA, did you participate in that?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What were the demands?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, it’s a long time ago, and I can’t remember the demands.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Was it related to compassionate use and parallel track? Or, were they already in place?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: It wasn’t one issue. It was many issues. We made a flyer – and it was many issues. I mean, we put down a number of issues.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did you have an affinity group with that action?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What was it?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I can’t remember.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did you get arrested?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, I didn’t get arrested.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Do you remember anything about that action?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: The buses, a lot of people there, people on top of the – someone having a banner on top of the projection of the building.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Iris, how much of your life was involved with this?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Quite a bit.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Ask your husband?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Would you say every day?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, every day. Every day, because I was either making calls – initially, there was no Internet or anything, so you had to make calls to find out about different drugs, drug companies, whatever. People would call sometimes, find out, I need this drug or whatever.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: People with AIDS would call you?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And ask for advice?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, that was going on, yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And did you feel comfortable giving advice?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: They were trying to get drugs, or – what the problem was with getting drugs. Actually, I was even contacted during the TB, by a patient who needed – because drugs were cut off, for some reason. They couldn’t get the drugs anymore, because the FDA banned the drugs, because they were contaminated or whatever, or they didn’t like where the drugs were coming from – for TB, certain TB drugs were unavailable. So, I helped a woman get drugs from Canada. She needed streptomycin – a very simple drug – one of the first drugs she needed. She only had one lung, and she needed this drug. It was part of her cocktail, and it was no longer available in this country.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What did you friends and family think? That you were spending all your time on AIDS?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, I had new friends, that’s all.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did your relationships change because of the work you were doing?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, I don’t think they changed. Maybe. I would have been doing something else, if I wasn’t doing this.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Were you talking about AIDS all the time – like, if you were getting together with your family, were you talking about AIDS?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. That was a time when I wouldn’t talk about AIDS that much. I would say what I was doing, but it wasn’t a long, drawn out thing.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, what about all these gay men? All these gay people that you’re spending every single day with – had you ever had gay people in your life, to that extent before?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Had you had any gay friends at all?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Not that I know of, no. It was very closeted, so it was very hard to say whether you did have a gay friend or not.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, how did that affect you? What did you think about that, at the time?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I sort of just accepted it, that’s it. I said, this is what I’m doing. These are the people I’m involved with. I like the people. It’s a whole different thing I’m doing here, and I think I’m doing the right thing, and I’m very interested in what I’m doing. So, that’s another thing. It’s getting drugs for people, and also, the whole idea of interacting. I was always a laboratory person, and now, interacting with people, it was completely different and something I had never done before. I was not a joiner before, at all. But, I was a fighter type person, that would fight for somebody’s rights.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What happened to you when people started to die – your friends?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, it was very hard on everyone – myself, the group. There were funerals, meetings, memorial meetings for people, and it was very moving, to see all the people that came.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did you have any particularly close friends, whose deaths you recall?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, one – I can’t remember his first name. His name was Bohn. He was a Quaker, and then another woman who died.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: From ACT UP?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, I think it was ACT UP, because I did get involved with some people – through someone in ACT UP, with a group of women in Brooklyn – it was a help group for women with AIDS – making them trainers and so forth. So, yeah, it was very moving, you know? To see people dying of this disease – knowing that they soon would not be here. There were a lot of people like that.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: You were the founder, I believe, of the AIDS Treatment Data Network?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Treatment Network. It was called ATR – AIDS Treatment Registry, and then the name changed a number of times. Then, it went AIDS Treatment Resources or something – AIDS Treatment.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What was the need that that responded to?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, you didn’t know where the trials were. I mean, my working with this one woman – the one woman who affected me, was this woman with ALS, and attempting to find the drugs. Now, in that disease – there’s no drugs for this disease. I even doubt if there are any drugs now. They were using cyclosporin or something. She went to Germany – she was German – there was nothing there. She came back and died shortly after. But, I know that this was an area that was not properly covered. The hospitals do not – or, the doctors do not get information about clinical trials out to people. And, there was a barrier, it seemed. You couldn’t give medical information, if you weren’t a doctor. There was all this stuff that you couldn’t do.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, you mean, individual hospitals would just be constructing their own trials, and nobody would know what anyone else was doing?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, it was another system that was set up – that didn’t work very well. It had to do with the doctors – the doctors in certain fields, whether they were in cancer or whatever. And, they would have to be research doctors. They would have to have certain qualifications and fill out the forms – the FDA forms, to be a principle investigator. Then, there were the drug companies involved with these doctors, too. If it was a drug company trial, there were payments made for these things. And they seemed to like to be under the covers.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: One can imagine that they felt comfortable with that system. They were getting paid in some way, shape or form. And, they didn’t want people to understand what was going on. It seems like this is what was going on. So, it was very easy to say, well, okay. I started to look at cancer trials, just to see what kind of data base there was – a government data base. And, I did find some stuff. But, I didn’t think it was very good or up to date or anything. It was very hard to get. So we said, well you have to have this type of information. This is crazy – keeping information from people, about where the drugs are being tested. That was the idea, it took off. Everybody was working on this – Bob Huff, everybody. We had meetings – that was another meeting – that was not Treatment and Data. And, it actually became overpowering, because the amount of work you had to do on this thing –

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How many clinical trials were there at a given time, that you would track? Like, in an issue of ATR or whatever?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, we got more and more, as the years went by. The first one – maybe there were 30, 40 or so, in the first book. One of the first books was in 1990. Then, it became more about pushing them. We got more trials. We were getting more trials. More drugs were being tested. When we pushed and finally got the ACTG, the AIDS Clinical Trial Group going, they were doing more trials, also. And then, we found out, it was very hard to get drug company trials, because that was more secret, because of all these payments probably going by, to the doctors. And finding – we were contacting each of the hospitals that were doing these trials, and you had to find the key person that would tell you what was going on there, in trials for AIDS. And, it was usually the same people that were doing the ACTG trials, actually. Some hospitals that are not ACTG sites – you had to make contact with the AIDS doctor there, and find out what the trials were. Or some coordinator.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, if you started out with 40 or 50 in 1990, what did you have by –

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I don’t know. I don’t know when I left ATR, but there were 60 or 70 trials.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And how often would ATR come out?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Initially, it came out – I don’t know if it was every quarter or whatever. We came out more often, and then we cut down because it was very intense. I didn’t like the fact that it was cut down. Nowadays, you can have it on the net, but we had to have hard copy, and it was very difficult.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, like, every three months, you’re coming out with a list of 60 or 70 trials. And, how extensive were the descriptions? Did you evaluate the trials? Or, did you just try to say what they were?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. All we did was give the entry criteria – for people who could get into it – blood work they had to have, and the sites where the trials were going on.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, this revolutionized AIDS research, because it democratized access to the trials – or at least information. So, ACT UP was running this also?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah. ACT UP was a nucleus of this happening, and it gathered the people who were going to work on this project. This became more intense I had to leave ACT UP somewhat – I had to leave Treatment and Data and only do this, because it was so intense.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: You left Treatment and Data to do the ATR?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Do you know what year that was?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I can’t remember. Maybe it was ’93, or ’94. No – it was before that. Probably, it was about ’90 – probably when the first directories came out.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: In 1990. And, how much longer did you stay in ACT UP after that?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, I continued to go to ACT UP.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Do you continue to go now?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, I don’t.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: You continued until when?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, I sort of – I don’t know how many years – it was about 1996 or ’97.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, you spent about 10 years in ACT UP?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Right. 10 years, definitely 10 years.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Okay, so you left T&D and you went to the ATR, around 1990. And then, you work on that for a few years.

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And, that was your major focus in ACT UP?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Did you work on anything else, later, in ACT UP? Or, did you stay with the Registry?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I pretty much stayed with the Registry. But, I was involved. I went to the meetings and stuff, and was still involved.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Can you describe, a little bit, how the introduction of the protease inhibitors or the ideas about the protease inhibitors – how they were received in ACT UP? And, when people first became aware of this direction?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Protease – yeah. I remember the first protease, which was a very small trial in Boston or somewhere. It was – essentially, it didn’t really give very much. I don’t know what protease it was, but it wasn’t that successful. But, I can remember that there was this small trial. I don’t know – it may have been at Johns Hopkins or somewhere, and everyone wanted to get in it. It maybe had 10 spaces. And, any new drug was really sought after, and people wanted to try it, get into the trial, whatever. And, that was, I would say, the beginning – that small trial of a few people. And, the protease probably is not around anymore. That was the model, and that’s what I remember was the first protease. And, of course, that was on Treatment and Data’s agenda – was the protease inhibitors, after that.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: When did you start to think that this could really be a turnaround direction?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, with the protease inhibitors, it just seemed to fall into place, all these things. This company makes it, that company made it; some other company made one. And, it just fell into place. And then, the nucleosides are still there, having cocktails. So, it’s the better use of the drugs – finding better ways to deliver what the dose should be. And, of course, measuring the viral load. Those are all the things that made sense with the drugs – reducing the side effects.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Were you involved with the campaign to change the CDC definition of AIDS?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Can you describe, a little bit, what that situation was?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, I can remember going down to the CDC – a rainy day, whatever it was, raining buckets – and changing the definition. And, one of the things that I helped to change there was getting TB as an opportunistic infection, I guess it was. And, the women’s issues that were there, also. And I was always interested in the women’s issues – the access to women in the clinical trials.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How were women excluded from clinical trials?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, they were excluded by the rules of the FDA, again. And the doctors – the research doctors. I can remember – this was before I even came here – this one doctor, when they treated rats, they only wanted male rats or something. So, it was very ingrown, with respect to – they felt that women’s bodies would affect the results in some way that they didn’t want because of the hormone cycles and everything – that they would affect these drug cycles and stuff. Like, no one else had these problems of hormonal things going on.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And it was really that vulgar? Those were the reasons why women were excluded from the trials?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, they didn’t say it like that, but that was the rationale they talked amongst themselves, I’m sure.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, how did that get that changed?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, Terry McGovern – and there were law suits against this. I can remember being called about women not being – one of the drugs, Ampligen, didn’t work very well, wasn’t a good drug, but the woman wanted to get into the trial, and couldn’t get into it. And, Terry McGovern sought these people out, and she worked as an advocate for these people.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: So, why did you finally leave ACT UP after 10 years?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: You have to move on. First of all, I did the AIDS Clinical Trial Group. I thought that was very important, to have a good Community Advisory Board – CAB, as they called it. And, I was always associated with Mt. Sinai, and I thought the CAB wasn’t going anywhere, so I thought I would take it over, and I became the Chair there. So, it was quite a bit of work, actually.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What were some of the projects that you did there?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Well, the whole idea was how you have a meeting every month and how you find out what’s going on, and also – you have to run – this is supposed to be a Board, and there’s supposed to be certain information given. Now, the investigator sometimes wants to give you his information. He’ll talk about – not AIDS clinical trial, not the government trials, but some other trial he wants to do. So, there’s a problem in what type of information, and also, how you train people, how the whole organization works and what influence you have at the national level. So, that took up a lot of time, figuring out that, and trying to – the CCG – the Community – do you know what it is? The CCG – it’s like the CAB on a national level – Community Constituency Group – that’s what it is. And, it’s supposed to be made up of representatives from the CABs and stuff, but that never really happened exactly that way. People may come from other areas. And so, there’s somewhat of a disconnect that I felt was a disconnect, between the CCG and the CABs. And, there’s a lot of issues – getting more members to CABs, and getting them to meetings and all these things. And, I tried to work in that area. I tried to drum up more activism in the CABs and help them get to meetings.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Who was in the Sinai CAB? Who were some of the other people?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: There was Holly Horn of ACT UP, and David – I can’t remember their names.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: David Gold?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: David Barr?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. I can’t remember right now. I have a whole list upstairs, if you need to know – Sandy Baker, who was a patient at Mt. Sinai. I built it up pretty good. Finally, there was even the woman who’s now in the CCG. What’s her name? Ann something. She works for the city. She’s a nurse, and she worked for GMHC, also. Holly acted as the Vice President and Secretary, and I was the Chair, and we had minutes at every meeting. I think they were too long, at this point, now, from what I know about minutes. But, we tried to record everything that was said at the meeting and we had good discussions. I was the Chair for two years there, and before that time, I was also involved – there was a man who had HIV, and he was a Chair. I just acted as a Secretary at that time, but I was sort of doing the work. He was not too well. And, I thought we built it up pretty good. We had regular meetings. There was never a meeting missed.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Now, when TAG separated from ACT UP, why did you stay with ACT UP? Or, did you also go to TAG?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No. I never went to a TAG meeting.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Why was that?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: I don’t know. I just felt – I didn’t feel – there was some sort of animosity between certain ACT UP people and TAG. I wanted to go, but I never pushed myself to go.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Were you ever in direct conflict with them?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: No, not exactly. Meetings are a dynamic. And, you can either feel wanted at a meeting or you don’t. And, I felt that some of the meetings, later on, were not very friendly. In fact, I saw one woman, who was a friend of mine – she was trashed. This had to do with peptide-T, and she was at the meeting and really made to feel not very welcome. So, I wasn’t comfortable with TAG. And, there were other people, also, that were not comfortable with TAG.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Right, so you stayed in ACT UP?

turns.speaker: SUBJECT
turns.text: Yeah, I stayed in ACT UP. The people are fine – Gonsalves and whatever, the others. But, there was a little ruthlessness. I don’t know what it was, there was something that was not just right.
